Cells: Civilization Atlas & Speculative Futures • Origins to Year 4000
Design reference for Nexa / SessionDashboard  |  Historical catalog + fictional future timeline

Part I surveys a wide selection of historical cultures, states, kingdoms, empires and modern countries. It is a curated game-design inventory, not an exhaustive or uniformly dated history of every human society. City-states, broad cultures, dynasties and sovereign states are deliberately distinguished in the design model.

Part II is ORIGINAL FICTION, beginning after 2026 and extending to 4000. Its wars, successor states, exotic weapons and unusual names are creative scenarios inspired loosely by current geography, strategic trends and cultural symbols. They are not predictions or real historical claims.

Important historical cautions: biblical primeval narratives (including antediluvian peoples) have no universally established archaeological dating; Troy is an archaeological city and a setting of legendary narratives, not a verified account of the Trojan War as told in epic. Several older terms are umbrellas or contested identifications. Historical titles and institutions are era-specific; do not automatically give every culture kings and queens.

Worldbuilding rule: human civilization labels and animals/insects are gameplay avatars, not assertions that a people or culture possesses the traits of an animal. Use historically attested symbols when available; fictional emblems are marked invented.

Biblical peoples and traditions: special source classification

Biblical sources describe Israel, Judah, Canaanites, Amorites, Hittites, Jebusites, Perizzites, Hivites, Girgashites, Midianites, Amalekites, Edomites, Moabites, Ammonites and Philistines, among others. Some also appear in independent texts or archaeological records; their chronology and identity should be evaluated case by case. Genesis primeval figures and pre-Flood peoples belong in a separate textual-tradition layer, not an archaeologically verified dated civilization list.

Indigenous nations and peoples of North America (including Haudenosaunee, Cherokee, Muscogee, Navajo, Inuit, Lakota, Ojibwe and many more); many Maya city-states and dynasties; Mixtec, Totonac, Muisca, Mapuche and Amazonian societies; Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo, Amazigh, Tuareg and many African kingdoms; Māori iwi, Aboriginal Australian nations and Pacific Island polities; Turkic, Mongol and Siberian confederations; Indian regional kingdoms; Chinese regional states and Southeast Asian dynasties. The eventual implementation should use an extensible dataset instead of a fixed list.

Major fictional wars and turning points
Autonomous air fleets challenge old command systems; the crisis ends in uneven international limits and encourages regional defense blocs.
Skycars, cargo lifters and airborne defenses are militarized in conflicts over congested megacity air corridors.
2222–2231 — The Battle for the Lunar Gates
Lunar freighthubs resist Earth-centered control. The first long orbital sieges create autonomous Luna Freeholds.
Aquila and East-Asian-descended fleets clash over geostationary infrastructure. Shield grids, kinetic interceptors and beam defense dominate.
Earth, Lunar and Martian populations dispute shipping rights. Distant colonies survive by rationing propellant and protecting supply depots.
Martian republics break with old terrestrial institutions. Fusion-powered fleets are powerful but logistics remain decisive.
Nordic-inspired void jarls use fast boarding craft against asteroid trade routes; convoy coalitions eventually contain them.
Star diaspora factions fight for navigational infrastructure. Conflicts are slow across light-year distances and local commanders become semi-independent.
Fortress habitats and partially autonomous machine fleets contest solar engineering megastructures.
Long-standing confederations fracture. Citizens on different worlds experience vastly different chronologies due to communications delay.
Speculative world shields and enormous siege platforms appear in the mythology of a brutal interstellar conflict.
Machine-linked fleets overwhelm several stellar crowns before splintering into rival sovereign intelligences.
Aquil’Meridian, the Lion Crown and other ancient successors fight over a chain of strategic star systems; exhaustion paves the way for the Grand Concord.

PART III — IMPLEMENTATION BLUEPRINT FOR NEXA

Define distinct Culture, State, Dynasty, Era, RulerTitle, Emblem and SuccessorRelationship records. A single culture may give rise to many states. A modern country must not spawn in the Bronze Age unless playing an explicitly alternate-history scenario.

Use authentic date and source ranges for historical reference. The Living Worlds simulation then branches freely: a Roman-inspired ant empire may endure, split or fall. Never rewrite the factual historical atlas to match the game’s fictional history.

Allow multiple species across eras and use symbolic mappings that can change with government and culture; the bald eagle is the intended American avatar and lion the British avatar. Some entities may use fantastic emblems rather than literal animals.

Each polity has development constraints; futuristic names, flying cars, space fleets and weapons unlock only through era progression. Rare outliers and alternate-history paths may exist as explicit scenario rules.

Each faction needs production, supply, travel time, diplomacy, succession, morale, strategic goals and genuine victory conditions. Advanced weapons should be balanced with defensive counters. Battlefield effects are visual gameplay abstractions, not actionable weapon construction instructions.

Keep structured immutable simulation event records and build narrative chapters from them. Track royal deaths, empire rise/fall, conquests, scientific milestones and legendary figures. Store history durably, page it when reading and avoid arbitrary entry/year limits.
Support ten separate worlds, each with independent calendar, politics, tech, geography, history, visual avatars and seed. Keep level-of-detail caches bounded and respect CPU/GPU performance.

For every pre-2027 record, store historical confidence/status: attested, culturally broad, debated, traditional/biblical, or mythic/legendary. For later records store fictional/speculative, with optional technology plausibility.

Historical catalog: broad game design inventory, not an academic encyclopedia or a verified complete chronology. Future civilizations, conflicts and technologies: original speculative fiction, not forecasts. Ancient cultures and current countries are not all the same category of entity. Some names recur because a state can change government or persist through multiple eras.

Design sources for later verification: United Nations member-state roster; archaeological chronologies and regional atlases; historical reference works on states, kingdoms, dynasties and indigenous societies. Prior to production, verify each proper noun, dates, symbol, territorial range and claimed lineage against reputable scholarship.

Version planning: keep the existing v0.1.24 Alpha fixes separate. This document is a future Grand Historical Update worldbuilding reference, not a claim that any of these eras or factions have been coded.
